title: POC scoping - benchmark harness integration
summary: POC scope for benchmark plan and harness integration. Discussed success criteria (latency SLO, throughput, cost targets), workload sizing (qps, concurrency, seq lengths), streaming vs non-streaming tests, and responsibilities for integrating Nova's scripts into Redwood's harness. Agreed on 2-week benchmark window after harness setup, AE to share template and security docs, SE to assist with test runs and metrics collection.
topics: Streaming vs non-streaming behavior and metrics

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-01-15
Time: 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Garber (Redwood AE), Priya Nambiar (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (Nova Head of ML), Rafael Ortiz (Nova Infra), Lena Park (Nova PM)

[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros and then we'll jump into the POC scope around the benchmark harness.
[00:18] Maya: Hi, thanks. Maya here. We're really excited to understand how Redwood can hit our p99 latency targets while keeping cost down.
[00:28] Alex: Great. Priya's our SE, she'll lead the technical details, I'll handle the project/ops side.
[00:34] Priya: Hi all. Quick note: feel free to interrupt. We'll want to map your production traffic profile to the harness.
[00:42] Rafael: Quick Q up front — we have both streaming and non-streaming inference in our stack, so we need to see both behaviours.
[00:52] Priya: Absolutely. That's a core part of the scope — streaming token latency versus batch non-streaming throughput. We'll capture both.

[05:10] Priya: Can you walk us through your workload? qps, typical sequence lengths, concurrency?
[05:20] Maya: Around 40 QPS baseline, peaks to ~180 during spikes. Sequence length average 120 tokens, p95 around 480 for some long context. Concurrency peaks at 30 simultaneous sessions for streaming.
[05:40] Priya: OK that's helpful. For benchmarking we'll want a distribution file — percents at different seq lens; that lets us pick right kernels and batching profile.
[06:05] Rafael: We can share a sanitized traceset and the request format. Our scripts are in Python (requests + SSE for streaming).

[09:00] Alex: Success criteria — what does success look like for Nova?
[09:06] Lena: Three things: p95 latency under 300ms for short responses (<80 tokens), p99 under 1.2s for streaming end-to-end, and cost not exceeding our current provider by more than 10% per 1M tokens. Also throughput must sustain peak bursts with graceful degradation.
[09:30] Priya: Noted. We'll capture token-level latency (first-byte, per-token), end-to-end latency for streaming, and per-token cost estimates. We'll also do quality checks to ensure model outputs match your baseline — we'll use your eval prompt set.

[12:45] Priya: About the harness — Redwood has a benchmark harness that can ingest customer scripts or run standard load generators. Typical integrations: 1) run your exact scripts inside a Docker wrapper we provide, 2) reimplement call patterns in our harness (JMeter-like), or 3) hybrid where we call your script as the request generator.
[13:02] Rafael: We prefer option 1 — running our actual scripts so we don't risk behavioral drift. They're using SSE for streaming. Are there known issues running SSE in the harness?
[13:22] Priya: SSE is supported but sometimes transcribes as chunked events; occasionally we see client timeouts if the harness default idle timeout is low. We'll configure keep-alives and token-flush intervals. Also, the KV cache — sorry I mean KV cache — sometimes mis-typed in our old docs as KV cash — might affect warm-start behaviour.

[17:10] Alex: On environment — do you want hosted Redwood API or Redwood Dedicated for this POC?
[17:20] Maya: We're leaning Dedicated because of data residency and performance determinism.
[17:27] Alex: Makes sense. Dedicated will give us predictable throughput and we can pin model variants. For security we'll share SOC2 and KMS integration docs.

[20:00] Priya: For the benchmark matrix we'll collect:
- throughput (reqs/sec)
- latency percentiles (p50/p90/p95/p99) first byte and last token
- per-token cost and GPU utilization
- streaming token interval latency and stitching latency
- quality deltas vs your baseline (BLEU/ROUGE or custom prompts)

[22:40] Rafael: About metrics collection — can we push metrics to our Prometheus?
[22:48] Priya: Yes, Redwood can emit Prometheus metrics or push to a pushgateway in the Dedicated env. We'll include label mappings for model/version/route. Also logs via secure log forwarder (we'll need a syslog endpoint or S3 with KMS).

[26:15] Maya: Timeline — what's realistic?
[26:22] Alex: Typical flow: 1) week 1 — harness setup and smoke tests, 2) week 2 — full benchmark runs and analysis, then a 2–3 day buffer for tuning. So ~2 weeks for the benchmark phase.
[26:40] Lena: That aligns with our timeline. We want results before the month-end exec review.

[30:05] Priya: Integration details: please provide your scripts repo or tarball, sample payloads, and a sanitized traceset. We'll run an initial smoke in our sandbox then port to Dedicated. For streaming we'll run both single-client long-session tests and concurrent multi-client tests.
[30:40] Rafael: Our scripts use requests + sseclient; and we also have a Go-based low-level client used in production. We'll provide both.

[34:12] Priya: On warmup — important for KV cache and model warms. We'll include warm-up phases and measure warm vs cold starts. For long context, model memory and kv cache sizes will matter for throughput.
[34:40] Maya: Do you support dynamic quantization? We're interested in int8/4bit profiles to reduce cost.
[34:50] Priya: Yes, Redwood supports several quantization profiles and we'll report quality regressions vs your eval set. We'll recommend profiles once we see traces and sequence distribution.

[38:00] Alex: Contract stuff — Rafael, will you need an NDA or security addendum before we run tests in your Dedicated?
[38:10] Rafael: We already signed an NDA last year; but we'll need the security addendum for KMS and network peering.
[38:22] Alex: I'll attach the security pack. Priya will include the network checklist.

[41:00] Priya: A few gotchas we've seen: 1) streaming tests can under-report latency if client-side buffering masks token timing, 2) bursty traffic needs careful autoscaling tuning, and 3) SLO targets need to specify which percentiles and token-length buckets.
[41:25] Maya: Good point — we'll provide buckets: short (<80), medium (80-300), long (>300).

[44:50] Priya: For the harness repo — we have a template Dockerfile and CI job. If you'd rather keep scripts private, we can run them in a customer-provided runner via VPN — Rafael you'd set that up?
[45:05] Rafael: Yes we can host a runner in our VPC, works for us. We'll need Redwood's runner image and instructions.

[47:30] Alex: Recap of commitments: Alex will send benchmark template, security docs, and sample harness config. Priya will prepare the harness branch and run initial smoke tests. Nova will upload scripts and dataset and provide access for the runner. Timeline: aim to have smoke tests by 2026-01-19 and full benchmarks the week of 2026-01-26.

[50:20] Lena: One small ask — can you include per-route cost breakdowns and token-level billing sample output?
[50:30] Alex: Yep we'll include a sample cost report and token breakdown.

[51:10] Maya: Thanks, this was helpful. We'll get the artifacts over.
[51:25] Alex: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with email and next meeting invite.
[51:35] (end)
notes: Customer prefers running their real scripts in Docker within the harness to avoid drift
Dedicated env preferred for deterministic performance and data residency
Success criteria: p95 <300ms for short responses; p99 <1.2s streaming; cost within +10% of current provider
references: Note: customer will upload scripts to shared S3 bucket or provide a runner in their VPC
